subject: zoology
question_text: Describe the structure of a cardiac muscle.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.33, SAQ 21). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. FIGURE SCOPE: this book prints a small shaded drawing of cardiac muscle beside the answer, but the question does not ask for a diagram, so the figure here is authored as a 0-mark study drawing, not a mark-bearing step.

steps.label: What cardiac muscle is
steps.why: Cardiac muscle is easiest to fix by contrast: it is striated like skeletal muscle but carries one central nucleus like smooth muscle, and it is the only muscle with branched fibres.
common_mistakes: Writing that cardiac cells are multinucleate. They have one nucleus, and it lies in the centre.
Calling cardiac muscle unstriated. It is striated.
steps.memory_tip: Cardiac muscle borrows from both: striped like skeletal muscle, one central nucleus like smooth muscle.
steps.margin_note: Where it is, cell shape, nucleus, striations. Four short lines.
lines: Cardiac muscle is the muscle of the heart wall.
It forms the myocardium.
Its cells are short and cylindrical.
Each cell has ONE nucleus, and it lies in the
centre of the cell.
The cells are striated: they show dark and light
bands.

steps.label: Diagram — cardiac muscle fibres
steps.why: The two features that name cardiac muscle — the branch and the intercalated disc — are shapes, so one small drawing settles them faster than a paragraph does.
common_mistakes: Drawing the fibres unbranched. Branching is the feature that identifies cardiac muscle.
Drawing the intercalated disc along the fibre. It runs ACROSS the fibre, where two cells meet.
steps.memory_tip: Draw a Y-shaped fibre first; the dark cross line where two cells meet is the intercalated disc.
steps.margin_note: The question does not ask for a diagram, so it earns no mark here. This book prints one beside the answer, and drawing it makes the branching and the discs obvious.

elements.caption: Step 1 — three muscle fibres side by side
Step 2 — the branches that join the fibres
Step 3 — intercalated discs across the fibres
Step 4 — one central nucleus in every cell

steps.label: Branched fibres and intercalated discs
steps.why: The branches connect the fibres into a network and the discs are the joints of that network, which is what lets the impulse travel in every direction through the heart wall.
common_mistakes: Confusing the intercalated discs with the striations. Striations run across the whole fibre; a disc marks the end of a cell.
Writing that the fibres are separate. They branch and join.
steps.memory_tip: Branched fibres make a net, and the intercalated discs are the knots of the net.
steps.margin_note: Branching and the discs are the two identifying features. Say the discs are found nowhere else.
lines: The muscle fibres are branched, and the branches
join the neighbouring fibres.
Where the ends of two cells meet there is a dark
cross line called an intercalated disc.
Intercalated discs are found only in cardiac
muscle.

steps.label: The heart muscle works as one unit
steps.why: The cells stay separate but behave as one because of the gap junctions, and that is exactly what functional syncytium means: joined in working, not in structure.
common_mistakes: Calling cardiac muscle a true syncytium. The cells stay separate; only their working is joined.
Writing that the nerves start the beat. The pacemaker starts it.
steps.memory_tip: Functional syncytium means separate cells, one beat.
steps.margin_note: Gap junctions, quick spread, one unit, pacemaker. Four short lines.
lines: The intercalated discs carry gap junctions.
An impulse passes through them from one cell to
the next without delay.
So the whole heart muscle contracts as one unit.
It is called a functional syncytium.
The beat itself starts in the pacemaker.

steps.label: Properties of cardiac muscle
steps.why: The heart may not stop and may not tire, so its muscle is placed outside the control of the will and is given the oxygen supply that prevents fatigue.
common_mistakes: Writing that the nervous system starts the beat. The pacemaker starts it; the nerves and adrenaline only change its rate.
Calling cardiac muscle voluntary. It is involuntary.
steps.memory_tip: Involuntary, pacemaker driven, adjusted by nerves and adrenaline, and never tiring.
steps.margin_note: Three properties close the answer. Do not repeat what is already written above.

lines.text: Involuntary, never tires, beats through life

lines: The heart beat is involuntary: it is not under
the control of the will.
Its rate is changed by the nervous system and by
adrenaline.
Cardiac muscle is highly resistant to fatigue,
so it works without rest through life.

insider_note: Three words carry most of this answer — branched, mononucleate and intercalated discs — and the last mark is usually lost by stopping before the properties.
